1. Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Federal Framework: Section 37 Deductions and Section 127 Investment Tax Credits

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program constitutes the cornerstone of the federal innovation architecture in Canada, supporting more than 24,160 businesses annually as the single largest federal source of industrial research and development support. Unlike discretionary grant mechanisms that depend on competitive intake cycles and finite budgetary envelopes, the SR&ED program operates as a statutory entitlement embedded directly within the Income Tax Act (Canada) (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Any corporation, individual, trust, or partnership carrying on business in Canada that executes qualifying scientific or technological work and satisfies the statutory filing requirements is legally entitled to claim the incentive.

Under the Canadian federal income tax system, the SR&ED regime delivers fiscal relief through two distinct, sequential statutory mechanisms that operate in tandem: the Section 37 Expenditure Deduction Pool and the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit (ITC). Pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool all qualifying current SR&ED expenditures—and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, qualifying capital SR&ED expenditures—incurred in Canada. Rather than capitalizing these outlays or amortizing them over multi-year schedules, the taxpayer may deduct the balance of the Section 37 pool in full against taxable business income in the current taxation year, or elect to carry any unused deductible pool balance forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Separately, subsection 37(2) of the ITA permits a current-year income deduction, without eligibility for pooling or investment tax credits, for current expenditures incurred on SR&ED carried on outside Canada, provided the foreign work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer, relates to a business of the taxpayer, and is solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer.

Operating alongside the Section 37 deduction, section 127 (specifically subsection 127(9) and related provisions) of the ITA enables taxpayers to earn a volume-based Investment Tax Credit calculated as a statutory percentage of their "qualified expenditures" for the taxation year. Depending on the legal status of the claimant, its prior-year taxable capital or gross revenue, and the nature of the expenditure, the federal ITC is granted at either a basic rate of 15% or an enhanced rate of 35%, and may be non-refundable, partially refundable at 40%, or fully refundable at 100%.

The interaction between Section 37 and Section 127 is governed by strict statutory anti-double-dipping rules. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments received, receivable, or reasonably expected to be received in the taxation year reduce both the deductible Section 37 pool and the qualified expenditure base used to compute the federal ITC. Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance that reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool in the current taxation year. Conversely, the federal SR&ED ITC itself is recaptured into taxable income, or deducted from the subsequent year's Section 37 pool, in the taxation year following the year in which the credit is utilized to offset tax payable or received as a cash refund.
1.2 The 2024–2026 Legislative Transformation: From Consultation to Bill C-15 Enactment

Between 2024 and 2026, the federal SR&ED program underwent its most expansive statutory overhaul since the 2012 Federal Budget reforms took effect in 2013 and 2014. For over a decade following January 1, 2014, the federal regime excluded capital property and capital lease expenditures from SR&ED eligibility, restricted the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for overhead to 55% of directly engaged salaries, capped arm's-length contractor inclusions at 80%, limited the basic ITC rate to 15%, and restricted the 35% enhanced refundable ITC exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) on a $3 million annual expenditure limit that phased out between $10 million and $50 million of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada.

Recognizing that inflation, rising hardware intensity in artificial intelligence and clean technology, and foreign tax competition had eroded the real value of those 2014 parameters, the Department of Finance initiated a multi-stage legislative reform process that culminated in the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Understanding the exact chronological progression from initial consultation to final enactment is vital for tax auditors and corporate practitioners, as interim policy announcements generated transitional figures that were subsequently superseded by the final statute.

During the Phase 1 and Phase 2 consultations conducted between January and June 2024, the federal government initially proposed a cost-neutral review before pivoting in Federal Budget 2024 to commit $600 million over four years. On April 25, 2024, the Department of Finance released a second-phase consultation paper with a stakeholder submission deadline of May 27, 2024, followed by further technical consultations in June 2024. This consultative process evaluated modernizing SR&ED eligibility parameters, extending enhanced refundable credits to Canadian public corporations, and establishing a Canadian "patent box" regime alongside accelerated tax depreciation for patents and rights to use patented information.

Subsequently, in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement released on December 13 and December 16, 2024, the Department of Finance unveiled a proposed $1.9 billion, six-year reform package applicable to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024). At that interim stage, the government proposed increasing the enhanced 35% expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million (which would have yielded a maximum $1.575 million refundable credit), raising the taxable capital phase-out thresholds to $15 million and $75 million, extending the 35% rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring capital expenditure eligibility for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024.

Before the Fall Economic Statement proposals were enacted into law, Federal Budget 2025 intervened to further expand the enhanced expenditure limit, raising it directly from the legacy $3 million ceiling—and superseding the interim $4.5 million proposal—to $6 million annually. Enacted via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, and retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), the law now in force doubles the maximum annual refundable federal ITC on current expenditures for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs from $1.05 million to $2.1 million.

body.text: 1.3 Macroeconomic Context and the Productivity Super-Deduction

The statutory expansion of the SR&ED regime under Bill C-15 does not exist in isolation; rather, it represents a targeted fiscal response to structural weaknesses in Canadian business sector productivity and intensifying cross-border tax competition. Economic surveys conducted by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in 2025 highlighted that Canadian per-capita GDP growth and business-sector labour productivity lagged peer nations, driven in part by lower small- and medium-sized enterprise (SME) adoption of broadband infrastructure, cloud computing, and capital-intensive automation. Simultaneously, the enactment of the United States One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) on July 4, 2025—which permanently reinstated 100% bonus depreciation for business capital expenditures and immediate expensing of domestic research and experimental expenditures—created acute pressure on the Department of Finance to prevent the migration of capital-intensive R&D and advanced manufacturing south of the border.

To counter this capital flight and complement the reinstated SR&ED capital expenditure credits, the federal government introduced the Productivity Super-Deduction (also referred to in practice as the Productivity Mega Deduction) alongside broadened Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) immediate expensing rules in late 2025. These non-SR&ED capital formation incentives interact directly with corporate R&D tax planning across three primary asset classes. First, under the immediate expensing rules for productivity-enhancing assets, businesses are permitted a 100% immediate first-year write-off on capital investments in patents and intellectual property, data network infrastructure, computer hardware and information technology equipment, and software and cloud computing infrastructure. Second, in addition to restoring Section 37 and Section 127 SR&ED eligibility for laboratory equipment, testing and validation apparatus, and specialized research technology, the broader productivity package supports immediate capital write-offs for dedicated research facilities and infrastructure. Third, capital expenditures on Canadian buildings acquired on or after November 4, 2025, qualify for immediate write-offs provided the building is placed in use for manufacturing or processing before 2030 and at least 90% of its floor space is used directly for manufacturing or processing activities. General capital assets outside these targeted classes—such as commercial real estate, non-zero-emission vehicles, and office furniture—benefit from a 50% enhanced first-year write-off under the Accelerated Investment Incentive.

The strategic consequence of this dual legislative track, which combines Bill C-15's restoration of SR&ED capital ITCs with the Productivity Super-Deduction, is a fundamental shift in the after-tax cost of hardware-heavy R&D in Canada. Prior to December 16, 2024, Canada's SR&ED regime heavily favoured pure software and labour-intensive claimants while penalizing capital-intensive sectors such as artificial intelligence infrastructure, semiconductor design, clean technology, aerospace, and biotechnology pilot plants. Under the post-Bill C-15 architecture, a CCPC or ECPC acquiring specialized graphics processing units (GPUs) or laboratory testing rigs after December 15, 2024, can simultaneously deduct 100% of the capital cost under Section 37 and claim a 35% federal ITC (40% refundable on capital property), fundamentally altering capital budgeting equations between capital ownership and operational cloud leasing.
2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and the Judicial Eligibility Framework
2.1 Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act: The Four Pillars of Eligible Work

The legal gateway to all federal and provincial SR&ED tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Drafted to align substantially with the international standards of the OECD Frascati Manual, subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Work only qualifies if it falls within one of three core scientific or technological categories—or constitutes enumerated support work directly tied to them—and does not fall within the statutory list of excluded activities.

The first two statutory categories encompass foundational scientific inquiry: paragraph 248(1)(a) covers basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, while paragraph 248(1)(b) covers applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third category, codified in paragraph 248(1)(c), covers experimental development, which means work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In Canadian corporate practice, experimental development accounts for the overwhelming majority of industrial SR&ED claims. Crucially, the statute distinguishes between the commercial objective (creating a new or improved material, device, product, or process) and the technological purpose (achieving a technological advancement that increases the underlying technology base or level from where it stood at the beginning of the project).

The fourth category, codified in paragraph 248(1)(d), governs eligible support work, which is restricted to work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to only eight exhaustively enumerated activities: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research. To qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d), such work must satisfy a strict dual nexus test: its scope must be "commensurate with the needs" of, and "directly in support" of, basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes commercial, routine, and non-scientific activities from the definition of SR&ED, even if they are conducted by engineers or scientists within an innovative enterprise. Statutory exclusions encompass market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes or cosmetic improvements; and routine data collection.
2.2 The Binding Common Law Test: Northwest Hydraulic and the Five Questions

Because the statutory language of subsection 248(1) is concise and principles-based, its legal boundaries have been definitively established by Canadian tax jurisprudence. The foundational judicial authority governing all SR&ED eligibility disputes in Canada is the landmark decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, authored by then Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman. In Northwest Hydraulic (building upon earlier purposive commentary in Conoltex Inc.), Chief Justice Bowman observed that Parliament enacted the SR&ED incentives to encourage scientific research in Canada, requiring courts to adopt a fair, realistic, and non-pedantic approach to interpreting the enacting provisions.

To operationalize subsection 248(1), Chief Justice Bowman formulated a five-question legal test that a taxpayer must answer in the affirmative, on a balance of probabilities, to establish that a project constitutes eligible SR&ED. First, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. If the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using generally available scientific knowledge, published literature, off-the-shelf software or hardware documentation, or standard engineering practice, no technological uncertainty exists. Uncertainty exists only when competent professionals in the field cannot determine prior to experimentation whether a given objective can be achieved at all, or which specific technological pathway or system architecture will overcome a fundamental limitation.

Second, the court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. A qualifying project cannot consist of unstructured trial-and-error or ad-hoc debugging; the claimant must articulate a testable scientific or technological hypothesis—an idea consistent with known facts that proposes a specific causal mechanism, architecture, or formulation to resolve the identified uncertainty. Third, the inquiry evaluates whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of the hypotheses. The investigation must be systematic, progressing logically from problem definition and hypothesis generation through controlled experimentation or rigorous mathematical and computational analysis, observation of empirical results, and iterative modification of the hypothesis until logical conclusions are reached.

Fourth, the court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. Crucially, under Northwest Hydraulic, a technological advancement does not require commercial triumph or a breakthrough unknown to the entire global scientific community; rather, it is satisfied if the experimental process generates new knowledge or advances general technological understanding for skilled practitioners—including conclusive proof that a hypothesized technological pathway cannot work, thereby eliminating a technological dead-end. Fifth and finally, the test requires that a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results be kept as the work progressed. Because the scientific method inherently relies on recording observations to test and refine hypotheses, the existence of contemporaneous technical evidence generated during the experimental cycle is a primary indicator of genuine SR&ED.
2.3 Administrative Evolution: CRA's 2021 "Why and How" Guidelines vs. Appellate Jurisprudence

For more than two decades following Northwest Hydraulic, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) structured its primary administrative guidance—including Information Circular IC 86-4R3, Interpretation Bulletin IT-151R4, and the now-archived Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy—explicitly around the five questions established by Chief Justice Bowman. However, on August 16, 2021, the CRA retired its archived eligibility policy and published the updated Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives.

The 2021 CRA Guidelines consolidated the analytical framework into two overarching administrative requirements designed to provide a simplified common language between claimants and CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs). The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement) evaluates why the work is being conducted—specifically, whether the work is undertaken to advance scientific knowledge (basic or applied research) or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement by overcoming a scientific or technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved through standard practice. The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search) evaluates how the work is being conducted—specifically, whether it proceeds by means of a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology through experiment or analysis. The CRA defines this systematic process through four mandatory operational steps: the generation of a hypothesis, the testing of that idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, the development of logical conclusions based on the results or findings, and the keeping of evidence generated as the work progresses.

A critical legal question immediately arose among tax litigators and auditors: did the CRA's 2021 administrative re-framing alter the substantive legal threshold for SR&ED eligibility in Canada? Both the CRA's own policy history and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) have definitively answered in the negative. The CRA explicitly acknowledges that both the two requirements ("How" and "Why") and the five questions are derived from the unchanged statutory definition in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. More importantly, in binding appellate decisions handed down both before and after the 2021 administrative revision—specifically C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72—the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed that the proper legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) remains governed by the five-question common law test articulated in Northwest Hydraulic. Administrative guidelines issued by the CRA are interpretive aids that do not carry the force of law and cannot narrow, expand, or override the statutory text of the ITA as interpreted by the courts.

body.text: Two recent Tax Court decisions merit deep technical scrutiny for corporate audit defence. First, in DAZZM Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129, the CRA sought to disallow SR&ED salary claims in part because the software claimant lacked granular, contemporaneous daily timesheets tracking employee hours by project. At paragraph 119 of the judgment, the Tax Court rejected the CRA's rigid administrative position, holding explicitly that while the CRA "would have liked to see contemporaneous time sheets for the work performed, they are not necessarily required for work to be eligible as qualifying SRED". While time-tracking logs remain the gold standard for minimizing friction during a CRA Financial Review, DAZZM Inc. establishes a critical legal safeguard: where a taxpayer lacks formal timesheets, the Tax Court will accept reconstructed time allocations supported by credible witness testimony, version-control commit logs (such as Git repositories), Agile sprint tickets, system architecture records, and payroll documentation.

Second, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159 (amended reasons for judgment dated January 17, 2025, regarding the 2020 taxation year), the Minister of National Revenue disallowed SR&ED expenditures incurred in developing a novel beverage formulation ("Chrisoda"), arguing that food and beverage recipe iteration constituted routine product development. Applying the five questions from Northwest Hydraulic and citing the purposive directive in Conoltex Inc., the Tax Court carefully distinguished between merely facing an uncertain commercial path toward an objective (which is insufficient on its own) and proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the underlying chemical and processing uncertainty could not be resolved through routine food science or standard procedures. Finding that Manning Canning formulated specific hypotheses, executed a disciplined scientific method, generated a technological advancement in general understanding, and maintained records of its trials, the Court allowed the appeal and referred the assessment back to the Minister for reconsideration and reassessment. This ruling underscores that non-traditional sectors—including food processing, agriculture, and light manufacturing—enjoy full statutory access to SR&ED when their experimental methodology is properly documented.
3. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Corporate Eligibility Mechanics
3.1 Tiered Rate Structure: CCPCs, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and Non-CCPCs

Under section 127 of the ITA, as amended by Bill C-15 (enacted March 26, 2026, effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), the federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit rate and refundability profile depend on four structural variables: the legal classification of the taxpayer, whether the taxpayer's qualified expenditures fall within or exceed its annual expenditure limit, the taxpayer's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada or three-year average gross revenue, and whether the underlying expenditure is of a current or capital nature.

A corporation that qualifies as a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) throughout the taxation year earns the enhanced 35% federal ITC on its qualified SR&ED expenditures up to its annual Expenditure Limit, which has a baseline maximum of $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—doubled from the pre-December 16, 2024 baseline of $3,000,000. Within this $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the 35% ITC earned on current expenditures is 100% refundable, generating up to $2,100,000 in cash refunds even if the CCPC has zero federal tax payable, while the 35% ITC earned on reinstated capital expenditures is 40% refundable. On qualified SR&ED expenditures in excess of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, a CCPC earns the basic 15% federal ITC. For a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income does not exceed its qualifying income limit, this 15% excess credit is 40% refundable; otherwise, it is non-refundable.

In a historic expansion of the regime, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—Canadian-resident public corporations whose shares are listed on a designated stock exchange and that are not controlled by non-residents—are now eligible under Bill C-15 to claim the enhanced 35% refundable federal ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures annually for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Qualified expenditures incurred by an ECPC above its expenditure limit earn the 15% non-refundable federal ITC.

Conversely, other corporations that are neither CCPCs nor qualifying ECPCs—including Canadian subsidiaries controlled directly or indirectly by foreign multinationals and large public corporations phased out of the enhanced limit—earn a flat 15% non-refundable federal ITC on all qualified SR&ED expenditures, with no ceiling on total claimable expenditure volume. Unincorporated businesses, individuals (sole proprietorships), and certain trusts earn a 15% federal ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures, of which 40% is refundable after offsetting federal tax payable. Finally, because a partnership is a flow-through entity rather than a separate taxpayer under the ITA, SR&ED deductions and ITCs are calculated at the partnership level and allocated to the partners, who generally claim the 15% basic rate according to their respective partner classifications.
3.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue Elections

The baseline $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit must be shared among all associated corporations using Schedule T2SCH49. Under the pre-December 16, 2024 statutory rules, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit was reduced when its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (aggregated across the associated corporate group) exceeded $10,000,000 and was completely eliminated at $50,000,000. (While a prior-year taxable income phase-out was repealed federally in 2019, it remains active provincially in Ontario for the OITC.)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 enacted two fundamental changes to the expenditure limit phase-out mechanics. First, for CCPCs applying the standard balance-sheet test, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit only begins to phase out when the associated group's taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, and is reduced linearly until it reaches zero at $75,000,000. Expressed mathematically, for a CCPC (or associated group) with prior-year taxable capital TC (where $15,000,000 < TC < $75,000,000), the adjusted annual Expenditure Limit (EL) for a full 365-day taxation year is: EL = $6,000,000 × ($75,000,000 − TC) ÷ $60,000,000.

Under this linear formula, every $10,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1,000. Once prior-year taxable capital reaches or exceeds $75,000,000, EL = $0, and the corporation may only claim the 15% basic federal ITC rate.

Second, because public companies often carry substantial paid-up capital and equity reserves on their balance sheets from public share offerings—even while remaining pre-revenue or early-revenue R&D enterprises, such as clinical-stage TSX or TSX-V biotechnology issuers or hardware scale-ups—Bill C-15 introduced a three-year average gross revenue test to govern the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phase-out for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). Crucially, Bill C-15 also permits CCPCs to formally elect to use this gross revenue-based phase-out structure in lieu of the taxable capital test.

This CCPC revenue-election mechanism operates as a high-value strategic tax planning lever. Consider a private Canadian clean-technology or semiconductor scale-up that has raised $45,000,000 in venture capital equity or convertible debt, which swells its taxable capital employed in Canada well above the $15,000,000 threshold and cuts its taxable-capital-based expenditure limit in half to $3,000,000, even though the company remains in the pre-commercialization stage with negligible gross revenue. By filing the statutory election to apply the gross revenue phase-out instead of the taxable capital phase-out, the CCPC preserves its full $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit and captures up to $2,100,000 in 35% refundable federal tax credits. Conversely, a mature, high-volume manufacturing CCPC with high gross revenue but low balance-sheet capital will retain the default taxable capital test.
3.3 Refundability Rules, Carryback/Carryforward Horizons, and Taxable Income Recapture

The monetization pathway for federal SR&ED ITCs varies sharply between refundable and non-refundable tiers. Qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn 100% refundability on the 35% ITC attributable to current SR&ED expenditures within their up-to-$6,000,000 expenditure limit. After first being applied to reduce any federal Part I income tax otherwise payable for the current year, 100% of the remaining credit balance is paid out directly to the corporation as a cash refund by the CRA. By contrast, a 40% refundability tier applies to three specific categories: the 35% ITC earned by qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs on reinstated capital SR&ED expenditures within their expenditure limit; the 15% ITC earned by qualifying CCPCs on current or capital expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit (provided prior-year taxable income is within the qualifying income limit); and the 15% ITC earned by unincorporated individuals and certain trusts. The remaining 60% of these partially refundable credits is non-refundable.

All non-refundable credits—comprising the 15% ITCs earned by foreign-controlled corporations, non-qualifying public corporations, and CCPCs above the qualifying income limit, as well as the 60% non-refundable portion of partially refundable credits—can only be used to offset federal Part I income tax payable. Pursuant to section 127 of the ITA, any unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years to recover prior federal taxes paid, or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to shelter future federal tax liabilities.

Under subsection 127(9), paragraph 12(1)(t), and subsection 37(1)(c) of the ITA, federal SR&ED ITCs that are either utilized to reduce federal income tax payable or refunded in cash are deemed to be government assistance received by the taxpayer. Consequently, the amount of the used or refunded federal ITC must be included in the taxpayer's taxable income in the immediately following taxation year (or, where the taxpayer has an undeducted Section 37 SR&ED pool balance, applied to reduce that pool in the following year). Because corporate income tax rates in Canada (approximately 9% to 12.2% combined federal-provincial for small business income, and 23% to 26.5% combined general corporate rate depending on the province, following the federal general rate structure of 15%) are substantially lower than the 100% value of the credit, the net after-tax retention of the federal ITC remains between 73.5% and 91% of the gross credit.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Allocation Methodologies, and Statutory Restrictions
4.1 Directly Engaged Salaries and Wages and Foreign Support Work

In the vast majority of Canadian SR&ED claims, employee remuneration represents the single largest component of qualified expenditures. Under subsection 37(8) of the ITA and paragraph 2900(2)(b) of the ITR, a claimant may include the portion of salaries and wages (defined in subsection 248(1) as income from an office or employment, plus employer shares of CPP/QPP and EI contributions where applicable under the traditional method) paid to employees for the time they were "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

The CRA enforces a strict functional test for "directly engaged" labour: eligibility is determined entirely by the hands-on technical tasks performed by the individual, not by the employee's corporate job title or academic credentials. If a software developer or mechanical engineer spends 60% of their working hours designing and testing experimental algorithms or prototypes to resolve a technological uncertainty and 40% of their time on routine code maintenance, user-interface styling, or customer technical support, strictly 60% of their salary qualifies for SR&ED. First-line technical supervisors who directly direct, review, and guide the technical course of ongoing experiments also qualify as directly engaged to the extent of that technical direction, whereas high-level executive oversight, human resources administration, financial accounting, and commercial project management are excluded from directly engaged wages, though partially captured under overhead.

For SR&ED support work performed outside Canada by employees of the Canadian taxpayer under subsection 37(2) of the ITA, the expenditure rules differ depending on whether the work is claimed solely as an income deduction or for ITC calculation. While subsection 37(2) allows a current-year income deduction for foreign current expenditures directly undertaken by the taxpayer solely in support of Canadian SR&ED, permissible foreign employee salaries included in the Canadian qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes are strictly capped at 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages paid to employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, and foreign contractor payments are entirely ineligible for federal ITCs.
4.2 Statutory Caps and Exclusions for Specified Employees

To prevent closely held corporations from artificially inflating refundable SR&ED tax credits by paying massive year-end bonuses or disproportionate salaries to owner-managers, the ITA and ITR impose stringent statutory restrictions on "specified employees". Pursuant to subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a specified employee of a corporation is any employee who is either a specified shareholder of the corporation—defined as a person who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time during the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any corporation related to it (including shares owned by persons with whom the individual does not deal at arm's length)—or an individual who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation (for example, a spouse, child, parent, or sibling of a controlling shareholder who works in the business, even if that family member owns zero shares). Because the test applies "at any time in the year," a startup founder whose equity stake is diluted below 10% partway through the fiscal year following a venture capital financing round remains a specified employee for that entire taxation year.

Three statutory limitations govern the SR&ED treatment of a specified employee's remuneration. First, under subsection 37(9) of the ITA, any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee is 100% excluded from qualifying as an SR&ED expenditure. The CRA defines a bonus as any payment in addition to the employee's normal, regular base pay. Furthermore, dividends paid to shareholder-founders do not constitute "salary or wages" under subsection 248(1) and never qualify for SR&ED. Second, under subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, the maximum SR&ED salary or wages that a claimant may include in its qualified expenditures for a single specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) (as determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee. For the 2026 taxation year, the CPP YMPE is $74,600, establishing a maximum direct SR&ED salary cap of $373,000 (5 × $74,600) per specified employee.

Third, when a claimant elects the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method to calculate overhead, subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the ITR further restrict the amount of a specified employee's SR&ED salary that can enter the PPA salary base to the lesser of two amounts: 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages from the claimant (comprising both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year); or 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual, with no proration for days employed when not a specified employee: PPA salary base = lesser of (75% × total salary or wages) and (2.5 × YMPE × days employed in the taxation year ÷ days in the taxation year).

For the 2026 taxation year (where YMPE = $74,600), the 2.5 × YMPE ceiling equals $186,500 for a full year of employment. Moreover, under subsections 2900(8) and 2900(10) of the ITR, if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (including deemed associated individuals or partnerships) in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the aggregate proxy salary base claimed across all associated entities for that individual cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500 in 2026). Finally, to satisfy CRA audit rules on accrued wages, any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year must be actually paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year; unpaid wages paid after the 180-day window are disallowed for the year incurred and cannot be included in the PPA salary base when subsequently paid.

body.text: Notice the subtle mathematical consequence of the 75% rule under ITR subsection 2900(7): if a startup founder is paid a regular salary of $100,000 and devotes 100% of their time to hands-on SR&ED, their direct SR&ED salary claimed is $100,000, but their PPA salary base is capped at 75% of $100,000 ($75,000), yielding a 55% proxy overhead of $41,250 rather than $55,000. Conversely, if that same founder devotes 70% of their time to SR&ED ($70,000 direct SR&ED salary), the entire $70,000 enters the PPA salary base because $70,000 is already below the $75,000 (75% of total salary) cap, generating $38,500 in proxy overhead.
4.3 Overhead Allocation: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method

Taxpayers must elect annually on Form T661 between two mutually exclusive methodologies for claiming SR&ED overhead and other expenditures: the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method and the Traditional Method. Under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method—used by the overwhelming majority of Canadian claimants due to its administrative simplicity and high notional yield—allows the taxpayer to add a notional overhead amount equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base (after applying the specified employee caps under ITR subsection 2900(7)) directly to qualified expenditures for the purpose of calculating federal and harmonized provincial ITCs. Under the PPA method, the taxpayer does not need to track or substantiate actual SR&ED-specific overhead expenses. While the notional 55% PPA amount is not added to the Section 37 deductible SR&ED pool, the taxpayer's actual overhead expenses (such as facility rent, utilities, support staff salaries, and travel) remain fully deductible as ordinary current business expenses under section 9 and paragraph 18(1)(a) of the ITA.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, no notional 55% salary uplift is applied. Instead, the taxpayer must itemize, track, and prove every dollar of overhead and other expenditures that are directly attributable and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada or to the maintenance of premises, facilities, or equipment used for SR&ED. Because the administrative burden of proving direct attribution during a CRA Financial Review is substantial, the Traditional Method is generally advantageous only for capital- or facility-intensive operations where direct SR&ED overhead significantly exceeds 55% of internal technical payroll—for instance, specialized contract testing facilities or operations relying heavily on external contractors rather than internal employees. Once filed with Form T661 for a given taxation year, the election between the PPA and Traditional Method is irrevocable for that year.
4.4 Materials Consumed or Transformed vs. Excluded Operational Utilities

Under paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR and the CRA's Materials Policy, claimants may include the cost of materials (including landed costs such as customs duties and freight) that are either consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed encompass physical inputs that are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a direct result of the SR&ED experimentation, such as chemical reagents, biological assays, or structural timber and composite samples tested to destruction. Materials transformed encompass physical inputs that are integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or new or improved product during the SR&ED process while retaining some residual commercial or scrap value. If an experimental prototype or transformed material is later sold commercially or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to (35) of the ITA claw back the lesser of the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value) and the original SR&ED material cost claimed.

Auditors must strictly enforce the boundary between eligible materials and ineligible supplies or general utilities. The CRA's Materials Policy explicitly excludes broken or used laboratory glassware and supplies, cleaning supplies, CDs and DVDs, used lubricants such as engine oil, and general facility utilities such as water, electricity, oil, and natural gas. An exception exists for a substance such as water only if the claimant proves that the water was directly consumed as a reactant or medium within the experimental process itself, rather than general facility plumbing, and documents the exact consumed portion using a reasonable, supportable, and verifiable allocation methodology.
4.5 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers (Form T1146), and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant engages external entities to perform SR&ED in Canada on its behalf, the statutory inclusion rate and documentation requirements depend on the legal relationship between payer and performer. Payments made to arm's-length Canadian subcontractors (corporations or independent contractors) for performing eligible basic research, applied research, experimental development, or support work in Canada on behalf of the claimant are fully deductible in the Section 37 pool, but only 80% of the eligible contract expenditure qualifies for the Section 127 ITC. The statutory 20% haircut removes the subcontractor's presumed profit margin and overhead markup. Furthermore, contractor payments never enter the 55% PPA salary base. To prevent double-claiming within Canada, if a Canadian contractor performs SR&ED under contract for a Canadian payer, the payer claims the 80% contract expenditure while the contractor's own SR&ED pool is reduced by the "contract payment" under subsection 127(9).

By contrast, payments made to a related or non-arm's-length person (such as a sister corporation or subsidiary) for performing SR&ED do not qualify as eligible contract expenditures for the payer. Instead, the non-arm's-length performer must incur the underlying SR&ED expenditures and may transfer those qualified expenditures to the payer only if both parties execute and file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length). Finally, third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED carried out in Canada qualify at an 80% inclusion rate for ITC purposes even though the claimant does not direct the day-to-day research, provided the SR&ED relates to a business of the claimant and the claimant is contractually entitled to exploit the results of the research.
4.6 Reinstated Capital Expenditures and the Cloud Compute vs. Owned Hardware Asymmetry

A central pillar of Bill C-15 (enacted March 26, 2026) is the restoration of capital expenditure eligibility for both the Section 37 income deduction and the Section 127 ITC, effective for depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024) and for lease costs that first become payable after that date. Restoring the general statutory architecture that existed prior to January 1, 2014, a claimant may include capital expenditures on new or used equipment, laboratory apparatus, specialized prototyping machinery, and computer hardware or GPU clusters—excluding buildings or leasehold interests in buildings—provided the property is intended to be used "all or substantially all" (defined by the CRA as 90% or more) of its operating time throughout its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or where lease payments for leased equipment are allocated to SR&ED use.

This legislative restoration creates a profound second-order tax planning asymmetry for artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), bioinformatics, and simulation-heavy enterprises regarding cloud computing versus owned or leased hardware. Renting elastic cloud compute or Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) environments (such as AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud) to train machine learning models or run simulations does not constitute a "material consumed or transformed" because no physical matter is consumed, nor does it constitute an "SR&ED contract" because the cloud vendor provides utility computing infrastructure rather than performing R&D on the claimant's behalf, nor is it a purchase or lease of tangible capital property. Instead, the CRA classifies operational cloud computing costs as overhead or other expenditures. Consequently, if an AI startup elects the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method—as most software firms do—its operational cloud computing bills are entirely subsumed within the 55% salary proxy and generate zero incremental SR&ED tax credits. The company can only claim actual cloud compute bills if it switches to the Traditional Method, forfeiting the 55% salary proxy and bearing the heavy audit burden of proving exact per-instance attribution of cloud servers to eligible SR&ED experiments versus commercial production hosting. (Alternatively, companies may seek direct non-tax grants under ISED's $300 million AI Compute Access Fund, part of the $2 billion Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy.)

By contrast, under Bill C-15, if that same AI enterprise purchases or leases dedicated GPU servers after December 15, 2024, and uses them 90% or more of the time for experimental ML model training in Canada, the hardware cost qualifies directly as a reinstated SR&ED capital expenditure. Critically, capital expenditures are claimed in addition to the 55% PPA on salaries. Thus, an AI CCPC buying $1,000,000 in GPU clusters can claim the full 55% proxy on its AI researchers' salaries plus claim the $1,000,000 GPU acquisition for a 35% federal ITC ($350,000 credit, of which 40% is immediately refundable in cash and 60% offsets tax or carries forward 20 years) and a 100% Section 37 deduction. Even if the hardware is used less than 90% for SR&ED, failing the SR&ED capital test, it qualifies for 100% immediate first-year expensing under the Productivity Super-Deduction.
5. Sub-National R&D Tax Regimes: Provincial and Territorial Analysis
5.1 Provincial Harmonization vs. Structural Holdouts Post-Bill C-15

In Canada's federalist tax system, ten provinces and territories offer sub-national R&D tax credits that stack atop the federal SR&ED program, while three jurisdictions do not offer an R&D tax credit. While most provincial R&D credits piggyback on the federal definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA and are administered directly by the CRA alongside the T2 corporate return—with the notable exceptions of Québec, administered by Revenu Québec, and Alberta, administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration—the provincial response to the federal Bill C-15 enhancements in 2025–2026 has been sharply uneven.

As of late 2026, corporate tax auditors must distinguish between Provincial Followers—such as British Columbia, which expressly aligned its regime with the federal Bill C-15 package for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, and Québec, which independently enacted its own sweeping CRIC modernization including capital expenditures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025—and Provincial Holdouts such as Ontario and Manitoba, which have retained their existing provincial expenditure caps, corporate eligibility restrictions, or capital rules rather than automatically adopting the federal $6 million limit or ECPC extension.

body.text: 5.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC Interplay

Ontario maintains a three-pronged R&D tax credit architecture administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario). First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit to qualifying corporations on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures, following its reduction from 10% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016. Crucially, as of late 2026, Ontario has not adopted the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit or the federal $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out corridor. Instead, the OITC remains capped at a $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit (generating a maximum $240,000 refundable credit) shared among associated corporations, which phases out linearly when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when its prior-year specified capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Furthermore, Ontario has not confirmed that restored federal capital expenditures are added to the OITC base.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) available to all corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario, regardless of size or CCPC status. Practitioners must note that a widespread typographical error in certain commercial summaries reverses the acronyms OITC and ORDTC; legally and statutorily, the OITC is the 8% refundable credit and the ORDTC is the 3.5% non-refundable credit. To prevent double-counting within Ontario, the ORDTC is calculated on the Ontario eligible expenditure pool after deducting the OITC claimed: ORDTC = 3.5% × (eligible expenditures − OITC). Both the OITC and the ORDTC constitute government assistance that reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool unless the taxpayer formally renounces the ORDTC or OITC on time. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures, up to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap, incurred under an eligible R&D contract with a qualifying Ontario post-secondary educational institution, hospital research institute, or non-profit research organization.
5.3 Québec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Consolidation and AI E-Business Credits (CDAEIA)

Québec operates the most autonomous and generous sub-national innovation tax regime in Canada, administered independently by Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Québec). In the Québec 2025–2026 Budget tabled on March 25, 2025, the Ministère des Finances du Québec enacted a sweeping structural overhaul known as the CRIC Revolution. Effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished and consolidated eight legacy R&D and design tax credits—specifically the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly claimed on Form RD-1029.7 at rates ranging from 14% to 30%), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1), the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03, subject to transitional utilization of existing eligible fee balances for tax years ending on or before December 31, 2029), the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, and the industrial design component of the In-House Design Tax Credit (retaining only the fashion design component)—into a single unified flagship incentive: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation, and Commercialization (CRIC).

The CRIC—claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T alongside the Québec CO-17 corporate return and Form RD-222 for the Québec R&D deduction pool within 18 months of fiscal year-end—transforms Québec R&D tax planning across five structural dimensions. First, it establishes a universal two-tier, 100% refundable rate structure: regardless of whether the claimant is a startup CCPC, a public corporation, or a foreign-owned multinational subsidiary with an establishment in Québec, CRIC is 100% refundable at a rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures above the exclusion threshold, and 20% on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 threshold. Second, beyond traditional basic research, applied research, and experimental development, CRIC expands eligibility to pre-commercialization activities that build directly upon R&D, specifically encompassing technological validation, pilot production, testing and studies required for initial regulatory approval or certification, and product or industrial design covering shape, aesthetics, functionality, and material selection.

Third, CRIC restores provincial tax credit eligibility for capital expenditures on R&D and pre-commercialization equipment acquired for use in Québec, including laboratory apparatus, software development infrastructure, prototyping machinery, and testing equipment, while excluding land and buildings. Fourth, the eligible cost base comprises 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees performing eligible R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec, 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for work performed in Québec, 50% of payments made to eligible public research centres, research consortia, or universities (whose recognitions continue to be issued by the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy), and eligible capital equipment purchases. Fifth, before the 30% and 20% CRIC rates apply, total eligible expenditures must be reduced by an annual Exclusion Threshold, defined as the greater of $50,000 overall or the Québec basic personal amount per employee (for example, $18,571 in 2025) prorated according to each employee's percentage of time devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. For instance, a Québec enterprise with 10 full-time R&D employees in 2025 faces an exclusion threshold of $185,710, meaning only eligible expenditures above $185,710 earn the 30% and 20% CRIC credit.

Alongside CRIC, Québec restructured its flagship information technology labour incentive. The legacy Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE)—which provided a combined 30% credit on eligible IT salaries, phasing down its refundable component from 24% refundable and 6% non-refundable in 2024 to 23% refundable and 7% non-refundable in 2025—was replaced for fiscal years beginning in 2026 by the Development of E-Business Tax Credit Integrating Artificial Intelligence (CDAEIA). Administered jointly by Investissement Québec (which issues mandatory annual eligibility attestations) and Revenu Québec, the CDAEIA provides a refundable tax credit of up to 30% on eligible AI integration salaries in the manufacturing, wholesale, retail, and information and cultural sectors. Québec further offers the Multimedia Titles Tax Credit (CDTIM) at up to 37.5% refundable and the Investment and Innovation Tax Credit (C3i / IITC) at up to 25% on manufacturing and computer equipment.
5.4 Western Canada: British Columbia Express Alignment, Alberta IEG, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba's Bifurcated Credit

Across Western Canada, provincial R&D incentives exhibit distinct statutory architectures. British Columbia (Form T666) provides a 10% SR&ED tax credit administered by the CRA. For qualifying CCPCs, the 10% credit is 100% refundable up to the expenditure limit and non-refundable on excess expenditures (which can be carried back 3 years and forward 10 years), while non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit. Uniquely among the provinces as of late 2026, British Columbia enacted express legislative alignment with the federal Bill C-15 reforms for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024: BC extended its 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), restored capital expenditures as qualifying BC SR&ED expenditures, and raised its prior-year taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000.

In Alberta, after eliminating its former 10% Alberta SR&ED tax credit effective January 1, 2020, the province introduced the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) for expenditures incurred after December 31, 2020, governed by sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and Information Circular IEG-1. Administered separately by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA), the IEG provides an 8% fully refundable base credit on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's historical base spending level (calculated as the average of eligible Alberta R&D spending over the two preceding taxation years), plus an additional 12% incremental credit—yielding a combined 20% fully refundable rate—on eligible expenditures exceeding that two-year historical base, up to a maximum annual expenditure cap of $4,000,000. The statutory filing deadline for the Alberta IEG is 15 months after the corporation's Alberta filing due date (21 months after fiscal year-end, which is 3 months longer than the federal 18-month cliff). Neighbouring Saskatchewan (Schedule 403), administered by the CRA, provides a 10% refundable R&D tax credit for CCPCs on up to $1,000,000 of qualifying expenditures and a 10% non-refundable tax credit for other qualifying expenditures, subject to an annual provincial cap.

In Manitoba (Schedule 380 / Section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba)), auditors must correct a pervasive error found in generic industry summaries that mischaracterize Manitoba's credit as a flat "15% refundable credit". Under Section 7.3 of the Manitoba Act, for expenditures incurred after April 11, 2017 (when the headline rate was reduced from 20% to 15%), the refundability of the 15% Manitoba R&D tax credit is strictly bifurcated. For in-house R&D not undertaken under an eligible contract with a qualifying research institute or post-secondary institution, 50% of the 15% credit is refundable (yielding a 7.5% effective refundable cash credit) and the remaining 50% is non-refundable (yielding a 7.5% non-refundable credit that can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years on Line 606 and Line 613 of Schedule 5). Conversely, for R&D performed under an eligible contract with a qualifying educational or research institution, 100% of the 15% credit is refundable. Manitoba's tax base independently includes current expenditures and depreciable capital property, excluding buildings and leasehold interests in buildings. Furthermore, Manitoba enforces two critical procedural deadlines: Schedule 380 must be filed within 1 year after the corporation's filing due date (18 months after year-end), and while a corporation may renounce the Manitoba credit provincially under subsection 7.3(7) up to 1 year after its filing due date, for federal SR&ED pool purposes, any renunciation of the Manitoba credit must be completed on or before 6 months after the corporation's tax year-end.
5.5 Atlantic Canada, Yukon, and Jurisdictions Without R&D Tax Credits (PEI, NWT, Nunavut)

In Atlantic Canada, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador all offer a flat 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit administered by the CRA on provincial SR&ED expenditures with no annual expenditure limit—claimed via Schedule 340 in Nova Scotia, Schedule 360 in New Brunswick, and Schedule 301 in Newfoundland and Labrador. Similarly, in northern Canada, Yukon (Schedule 442) provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit administered by the CRA on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in the territory, plus an additional 5% fully refundable credit (for a combined 20% refundable rate) on eligible amounts paid or payable to Yukon University (formerly Yukon College).

A mandatory audit verification point involves correcting third-party marketing tables that erroneously list Prince Edward Island (PEI) as having a "15% refundable SR&ED credit". Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do NOT have a provincial or territorial SR&ED income tax credit. While PEI offers a separate Prince Edward Island Corporate Investment Tax Credit (Schedule 321) for qualified manufacturing and processing property, R&D claimants in PEI rely on the federal SR&ED credit supplemented by discretionary non-repayable innovation grants administered by Innovation PEI. Similarly, claimants in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut rely on federal SR&ED alongside territorial grant programs or 15% investor credits under the Risk Capital Investment Tax Credits Act.
6. Interaction with Direct Innovation Grants and Stacking Mathematics
6.1 Government Assistance Reductions Under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(9)

While Canadian businesses routinely combine ("stack") direct government grants, interest-free repayable contributions, and provincial R&D tax credits with federal SR&ED claims, the Income Tax Act prevents a taxpayer from earning federal SR&ED tax credits on expenditures that have already been reimbursed or subsidized by another public source. Under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the ITA (and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy), any "government assistance"—defined broadly to include any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, or investment allowance from a federal, provincial, or municipal government or public authority—received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received in respect of SR&ED reduces both the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and the qualified expenditure base on which the federal ITC is calculated. If a taxpayer subsequently repays government assistance—such as repaying a conditional contribution from a regional development agency—subsection 37(1)(c) and subsection 127(10.8) restore the repaid amount to the SR&ED expenditure pool in the year of repayment.

Crucially, when a claimant uses the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method for overhead, a direct salary grant—such as an NRC IRAP contribution that reimburses 60% to 80% of an R&D employee's wages—does not reduce the employee's gross SR&ED salary prior to calculating the 55% proxy. Instead, the employee's full SR&ED salary still enters the PPA salary base to generate the full 55% notional overhead proxy, and the IRAP grant is deducted afterward from the aggregate pool of qualified expenditures. This statutory mechanic makes stacking NRC IRAP with PPA-based SR&ED highly lucrative for Canadian SMEs.

6.3 Multi-Jurisdictional Stacking Models and Net Effective Subsidy Rates

Because provincial R&D tax credits reduce the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base as government assistance under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the combined effective tax credit rate is not a simple arithmetic sum of the federal and provincial percentages; rather, it follows a sequential reduction formula: combined rate = provincial rate + federal rate × (1 − provincial rate).

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics across Canada's three largest innovation hubs in 2026, consider a qualifying CCPC (with prior-year taxable capital under $10,000,000) that incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged non-specified employee SR&ED salaries and zero contractor or material costs while electing the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method.

In Ontario, the CCPC starts with $1,000,000 in gross SR&ED salaries and adds the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount of $550,000 to establish gross qualified expenditures before assistance of $1,550,000. The corporation first claims the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) on $1,550,000, yielding $124,000. Next, the corporation computes the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario R&D Tax Credit (ORDTC) on the OITC-reduced base of $1,426,000 ($1,550,000 − $124,000), yielding $49,910. Deducting both Ontario credits from $1,550,000 leaves a net federal qualified expenditure base of $1,376,090, which earns a 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC of $481,631.50. Summing the federal and Ontario credits yields $655,541.50 in total tax credits—representing 65.55% of actual cash salary outlay, of which $605,631.50 (60.56%) is immediately refundable in cash. If the Ontario CCPC has no Ontario income tax payable and elects to formally renounce the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC, its net federal base rises to $1,426,000, increasing its 35% refundable federal cash credit to $499,100 and yielding $623,100 (62.31%) in 100% refundable cash.

In British Columbia, a CCPC or ECPC with $1,000,000 in SR&ED salaries and $550,000 in 55% proxy overhead starts with the same $1,550,000 gross qualified expenditure pool. It claims the 10% refundable BC SR&ED Tax Credit of $155,000, which reduces the net federal qualified expenditure base to $1,395,000. Applying the 35% refundable federal ITC rate to $1,395,000 yields $488,250, resulting in a combined federal and BC cash refund of $643,250, or 64.33% of actual cash salary outlay in 100% refundable cash.

In Québec, under the post-March 25, 2025 CRIC regime, a CCPC or ECPC employing 10 full-time R&D personnel at $100,000 each ($1,000,000 gross SR&ED salaries) first applies the Québec CRIC exclusion threshold of $185,710 (10 × $18,571 basic personal amount), leaving $814,290 in net Québec eligible salaries (as Québec calculates CRIC on direct salaries without the federal 55% notional proxy). Because this amount falls within the first $1,000,000 above the threshold, it earns the 30% Tier-1 refundable CRIC rate, generating $244,287 in refundable Québec credits. For federal purposes, the company's $1,550,000 gross pool ($1,000,000 salaries plus $550,000 PPA) is reduced by the $244,287 CRIC government assistance to $1,305,713, which earns a 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC of $456,999.55. Together, the combined federal SR&ED and Québec CRIC cash refund reaches $701,286.55—representing 70.13% of actual cash salary outlay in 100% refundable cash, prior to layering any additional AI integration salary credits under CDAEIA.

body.text: 7. Governance, Filing Procedures, Statutory Deadlines, and Audit Defence
7.1 Governing Authorities, Prescribed Tax Forms, and the 18-Month Statutory Cliff

The administration of the federal SR&ED program is vested in the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), while legislative policy resides with the Department of Finance Canada. To perfect a valid SR&ED claim, a taxpayer must file the prescribed technical and financial schedules with its income tax return. The primary federal filing instrument is Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), which was revised in 2026 to incorporate the Bill C-15 capital expenditure restoration and amended expenditure limit elections. Part 2 of Form T661 requires project-by-project technical descriptions addressing the scientific or technological uncertainties, hypotheses formulated, systematic experimentation conducted, and technological advancements achieved within strict CRA word limits.

Alongside Form T661, corporate claimants must submit Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations)—while individuals and trusts submit Form T2038(IND)—to compute the federal ITC, expenditure limit phase-out, refundability, and carryback or carryforward balances. Associated corporate groups must file Schedule T2SCH49 to allocate the $6,000,000 SR&ED expenditure limit among associated corporations, and non-arm's-length contracting parties must file Form T1146 to transfer qualified expenditures. At the sub-national level, claimants must file the corresponding provincial or territorial schedules: Form T666 for British Columbia, Schedule 508 and Schedule 568 for Ontario, Form CO-17 accompanied by Form RD-1029.8.CR-T and Form RD-222 for Québec (filed directly with Revenu Québec), Schedule 380 for Manitoba, Schedule 403 for Saskatchewan, Schedule 340 for Nova Scotia, Schedule 360 for New Brunswick, Schedule 301 for Newfoundland and Labrador, Schedule 442 for Yukon, and the Alberta IEG Claim Form filed with Alberta TRA.

Pursuant to subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the ITA, a taxpayer's prescribed SR&ED forms containing the prescribed information for an expenditure must be filed on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing due date for the taxation year. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year, the corporate SR&ED filing deadline is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year—for example, a corporation with a December 31, 2025 fiscal year-end has a T2 filing due date of June 30, 2026, and an absolute SR&ED deadline of June 30, 2027. For individuals and trusts, the deadline is 12 months after the income tax filing due date for the year, and for partnerships, it is 12 months after the partnership's fiscal period end (or 12 months after the earliest filing due date of the members). This 18-month corporate deadline operates as a strict statutory bar ("the 18-month cliff"). Neither the CRA nor the Tax Court of Canada possesses discretionary authority under the fairness provisions of the ITA to grant an extension or accept an SR&ED claim—or allow upward amendments to claimed expenditure line items on Form T661—submitted even one day after the 18-month window expires.
7.2 CRA Technical and Financial Review Protocols, SALT, and the April 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process

The CRA conducts detailed technical and financial reviews (audits) on approximately 20% of all SR&ED claims filed annually. During an audit, the CRA assigns two specialized officers who evaluate the claim independently. The Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), a domain scientist or engineer, conducts the Technical Review, evaluating whether the claimed projects satisfy the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) and the five Northwest Hydraulic questions. Concurrently, the Financial Reviewer (FR), a tax auditor, conducts the Financial Review, verifying general ledger reconciliation, payroll T4 summaries, specified employee ownership and cap tables, 180-day payment proof, contractor statements of work, material consumption logs, and government assistance deductions.

To assist SMEs and first-time claimants in evaluating project eligibility prior to filing, the CRA operates the online Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT), which replaced the earlier Eligibility Self-Assessment Tool (ESAT). More significantly, as part of the federal SR&ED modernization package, on April 1, 2026, the CRA officially launched a Voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process. Under this program, corporate claimants may submit project protocols and technical documentation to the CRA prior to filing their annual tax return to obtain upfront administrative certainty on whether their R&D projects satisfy subsection 248(1), substantially reducing post-filing audit risk and enabling businesses to finance R&D receivables with higher confidence.
7.3 Contemporaneous Documentation Standards and Audit Risk Mitigation

Inadequate contemporaneous documentation is the single primary cause of SR&ED claim reductions and disallowances during CRA reviews. Retroactively reconstructing technical narratives at the end of the fiscal year without underlying evidence created during the experimental work invites immediate RTA skepticism. To survive a combined CRA Technical and Financial Review, corporate taxpayers must maintain two synchronized evidentiary trails generated as the R&D progresses.

On the technical evidence trail, claimants should preserve project planning documents, design of experiments (DoE), system architecture diagrams, source code version-control commit logs with technical commit messages explaining failed builds or performance bottlenecks, records of trial runs, laboratory notebooks, benchmark test datasets, photographs or videos of failed physical prototypes, and internal engineering post-mortems, ensuring that every artifact maps directly to a formulated hypothesis and an empirical test result. On the financial evidence trail, claimants should maintain project-level time-tracking logs or Agile sprint allocations (noting that while DAZZM Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129, confirms timesheets are not an absolute statutory prerequisite, they remain the most effective shield against arbitrary audit reductions), complete corporate cap tables showing exact dates of share issuances to verify specified employee status, arm's-length contractor agreements explicitly detailing the Canadian SR&ED statement of work and intellectual property terms, material scrap and consumption logs, and asset utilization logs proving 90% or greater SR&ED operating time for reinstated capital equipment acquired after December 15, 2024.
8. Strategic Conclusions and Compliance Recommendations for Corporate Taxpayers

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 (retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), alongside Québec's transition to the unified CRIC regime after March 25, 2025, and the introduction of the federal Productivity Super-Deduction, has fundamentally re-engineered the economics of industrial R&D in Canada. To maximize non-dilutive capital recovery while maintaining rigorous audit compliance, corporate tax directors, chief financial officers, and R&D leaders should execute a cohesive five-part compliance and optimization strategy.

First, capital-intensive CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada falls within or exceeds the new $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 phase-out range—for example, due to large venture capital equity rounds or debt facilities on the balance sheet—must immediately model the newly enacted three-year average gross revenue election under Bill C-15. Similarly, public technology and life-sciences issuers must evaluate their qualification as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) to capture up to $2,100,000 in 35% refundable federal credits on the doubled $6,000,000 expenditure limit.

Second, with capital expenditures restored under Bill C-15 for property acquired after December 15, 2024, acquiring or leasing dedicated GPU clusters, laboratory apparatus, and prototyping equipment now generates both a 100% Section 37 deduction and a 35% (or 15%) federal ITC without eroding the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount on salaries. Because operational cloud computing costs remain trapped inside the 55% notional overhead proxy unless the taxpayer elects the Traditional Method, hardware-intensive AI and cleantech enterprises should evaluate shifting predictable baseline compute workloads from rented cloud instances to owned or capital-leased Canadian hardware.

Third, multi-provincial corporations must account for the sharp divergence between aligned provinces (British Columbia and Québec) and holdout provinces (Ontario and Manitoba). In Ontario, where the 8% refundable OITC remains capped at $3,000,000, pre-profit CCPCs that cannot utilize the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC should evaluate renouncing the ORDTC to prevent it from reducing their 35% refundable federal SR&ED base. In Manitoba, corporations intending to renounce the non-refundable half (7.5%) of the Manitoba credit for federal pool purposes must do so within 6 months after fiscal year-end, rather than waiting until the 18-month Schedule 380 filing deadline.

Fourth, enterprises operating in Québec for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, must expand their internal project tracking beyond narrow subsection 248(1) experimental development to capture newly eligible pre-commercialization activities—including regulatory certification testing, technological validation, pilot production, and industrial or product design—as well as Québec capital equipment under the 30% and 20% refundable CRIC regime, while structuring employee time allocations to optimize the per-employee exclusion threshold.

Fifth and finally, for large, high-risk, or novel R&D initiatives, taxpayers should utilize the CRA's Voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process launched on April 1, 2026, to lock in technical eligibility upfront. Simultaneously, engineering teams should embed lightweight, automated documentation habits into existing workflows—linking Git commits, Jira tickets, and test logs directly to technological uncertainties and hypotheses—while ensuring payroll structures for founder-shareholders who are specified employees strictly avoid ineligible bonuses in favour of regular base salary up to the 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500) proxy ceiling and 5 × YMPE ($373,000) direct salary ceiling.
